Hand, foot, and mouth disease

Painful stomatitis lasted a mean 4.0 days with LLLT versus 6.7 days with placebo in one small trial. The study did not test viral clearance or total illness duration.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Painful stomatitis lasted a mean 4.0 days with LLLT versus 6.7 days with placebo in one small trial. The study did not test viral clearance or total illness duration.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact category contains one human randomized, double-blind trial (20 participants) of 830-nm LLLT for painful stomatitis; no other exact-category publication is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

Daily treatment for 4–7 days shortened the painful period versus placebo (4.0±1.3 vs 6.7±1.6 days); 90% accepted treatment and no adverse events were reported (Toida et al. 2003). The trial addresses palliation of oral pain rather than viral clearance, contagiousness, fever, neurologic complications, or total disease duration. Because hand-foot-and-mouth disease is usually self-limited and the sample was small, the absolute difference should be interpreted as a preliminary symptom-control signal. The database provides no independent replication, no alternative-dose comparison, and no information on recurrence or rare adverse events. Treatment acceptability in this cohort and the absence of reported adverse events do not establish safety in larger pediatric populations. Accordingly, the finding cannot be generalized to infants, severe enteroviral disease, or routine antiviral management.

Primary original study: Toida et al. 2003

none identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

none identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The trial used 830 nm near-infrared light at 1.1 J/cm² for 30 seconds daily over 4–7 days. This is outside the visible spectrum. The report concerns painful oral lesions in the studied children; its schedule does not establish effects on viral clearance, contagiousness, or severe enteroviral disease.

Interpretation

The result is a preliminary symptom-control signal from one small trial. Hand, foot, and mouth disease is self-limited, and the report does not establish a role for PBM in managing infection or complications. No independent replication or larger safety estimate is available from this category.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow. One small randomized double-blind trial found shorter stomatitis pain duration.
Publications and records1 unique title.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial evaluated low-level laser treatment for painful stomatitis in 20 participants. The treated group had a shorter pain period than placebo, but the sample was small and the indication is symptom control during a self-limited infection. Independent replication and evidence for other disease outcomes are absent.
